intro: In June of Year 1, every child in England takes the Phonics Screening Check (PSC) — a short, simple check of one thing: can your child sound out and blend words? It does not test understanding or speed. This page explains what actually happens, so there is nothing to worry about.

paras: The check looks only at whether your child can use phonics to decode words — it does not test whether they understand what a word means, and it is not timed.

Your child reads 40 words aloud, one-to-one, to an adult they already know well (usually their own teacher) — never a stranger, and never remotely. Half the words are real words; half are made-up "nonsense words", each shown with a picture of an imaginary creature so your child knows straight away it is not a real word and should simply be decoded, not recognised by sight.
There are a few practice words first, which are not scored, so your child always knows what to expect before the real check begins. Most children take somewhere between about 4 and 9 minutes.

The exact number of words needed to meet the expected standard is set freshly each year and is not published until after the check — it is not the same number every year, so please ignore any specific number you might see online for a previous year.

sections.h: How we prepare your child — and how we don’t
paras: We do not drill long lists of nonsense words — the official guidance is clear that this does not actually help. Instead, we keep teaching and practising the normal Wren Phonics sequence, which already includes real decodable words and the occasional nonsense word built from sounds already taught, in the same untimed, one-to-one style as the real check, so the FORMAT feels familiar on the day, not just the content.

sections.h: If the expected standard isn’t met
paras: This is common and nothing to be alarmed about — a meaningful number of children do not meet the standard in Year 1 every year. Your child simply continues phonics teaching and support into Year 2, and retakes the check the following June alongside that year’s Year 1 children. We will always tell you your child’s result and what support we are putting in place, as all schools are required to.

Children who need it can have rest breaks, larger print or fewer words on each page, a coloured overlay, or other normal classroom adjustments. A child who usually draws sound buttons can draw them on a clean copy of the words (the teacher cannot draw them for them). These do not need special permission if they are what that child uses day to day anyway. Talk to your child’s teacher if you think your child may need one of these.
